kurz: Why the answer is already settled before thinking begins, and what switches on slow thinking.

bloecke.md:
A share price falls by 4%, and the portfolio app reports it at 7:12. Even before the notification has been read to the end, the answer is already settled: sell the position. This answer is there before any weighing of pros and cons. The thinking that sets in afterwards merely supplies a justification for it. A justification can be found for any answer that is already settled.

In 2011 Daniel Kahneman described this division of labour using two names that he adopted from the psychologists Keith Stanovich and Richard West (2000). **[[System 1]]** works quickly, automatically, associatively and without noticeable effort. It is constantly active and has an immediate answer to almost everything. **[[System 2]]** works slowly, according to rules and step by step. It takes effort, is therefore used as rarely as possible and normally accepts unchecked whatever System 1 presents to it. Kahneman repeatedly stressed that both systems are fictitious characters. They serve as a linguistic aid and do not denote places in the brain.

System 1 answers first, and System 2 then supplies the justification. Better decisions require interrupting this sequence before the answer is settled. Once the justification is complete, the decision can hardly be changed any more.

## Conditions for reliable intuition

Most everyday thinking runs through System 1, and that is not a flaw. Reading, driving, interpreting faces or sensing the mood in a room would not work at all under conscious control.

Kahneman and Gary Klein, who had spent decades observing how firefighters and nurses make decisions, long held opposing positions on this. In 2009 they agreed on two conditions under which intuition becomes reliable. First, the environment must be regular enough for there to be anything to learn at all. Second, you must have learned this regularity through many repetitions with quick, unambiguous feedback. If either condition is missing, self-confidence develops anyway, but without the skill that should go with it. This case is dangerous because, to the person concerned, it feels exactly like genuine competence.

bloecke.unter: Reliable intuition requires a regular environment and many repetitions with clear feedback (Kahneman/Klein 2009).

felder.text: Picking individual shares, market timing, selecting funds by past performance. Feels like experience but produces no verifiable skill.
Driving, chess, operational experience in the fire service and the emergency department. Here System 1 may decide.
Buying a property, a pension contract, an inheritance. One-off, consequential, no learning curve. A task for System 2 and for advice.
Tax return, choosing the right order type, setting up a savings plan. Rarely practised, but a mistake shows up immediately and can be corrected.

bloecke.md:
## Learning conditions on the stock exchange

After a game of chess, it is clear whether a move was good. After a sale, by contrast, nothing is clear, because although the price keeps moving, it does not show whether the decision was right. A carefully reasoned decision can cost money, and a rash order can pay off. Both experiences shape intuition in the same way. The feedback comes late, is overlaid by chance and often points in the wrong direction. In addition, situations do not repeat themselves closely enough. Every market situation differs so much from earlier ones that an old rule no longer applies. What feels like twenty years of experience is therefore often one year of experience repeated twenty times.

Kostolany described this without psychological jargon. He attributed short-term price movements almost entirely to mood and only to a small extent to facts.

## Swapping difficult questions

System 1 replaces difficult questions with easier ones. Kahneman calls this **[[Attribute substitution|attribute substitution]]**. In this way, “How will this company develop over ten years?” becomes the question “Do I like this company?”, and “How likely is a slump?” becomes the question “How easily does a slump come to mind?” The substitute question is answered correctly, the result feels complete, and the swap goes unnoticed. That is why it is so hard to correct.

The [[Action bias|action bias]] follows the same pattern. “Is acting better than doing nothing?” becomes “How well can I bear doing nothing?”

bloecke.md:
## Limits of knowing about cognitive biases

The obvious countermeasure, learning about cognitive biases and then watching out for them, works poorly. In the wheel-of-fortune experiment of 1974, all participants saw how the number was determined, seemingly at random (the wheel was set so that it only stopped at 10 or 65). Nevertheless, it shifted the median of the estimates by twenty percentage points. This is where the [[Bias blind spot|bias blind spot]] shows. An effect is easy to recognise in others and hardly at all in yourself.

Two measures have a measurable effect. The first is rephrasing. If the same task is posed in frequency format (“out of 100 cases like this one, how many?”), the error rate in the Linda problem falls from around 85% to around 20%. The second is the default setting. In 2003 Johnson and Goldstein compared the willingness to donate organs. In Germany, with opt-in (active consent required), 12% consented; in Austria, with opt-out (active objection required), 99.98% did. A single cross on a form thus made a difference of almost 88 percentage points. Applied to investing, this means that a running savings plan achieves more than any good intention.

The statement “I know the effect, so I don't have it” is a consequential error. Knowing about biases barely changes your own behaviour. Above all, it improves the ability to recognise them in others. What works are rules that are fixed before the emotion arises. Attentiveness in the moment, by contrast, helps little.

## Three measures that switch on System 2

All three take effect before the answer is settled, not only afterwards.

- A delay separates impulse and execution. A fixed waiting period between decision and order costs nothing and filters out every decision that only looked good for a day.
- Putting things in writing requires a justification before any action is taken. A consideration that cannot be written down in three sentences is more of a mood than a thesis.
- Translating into numbers takes away a story's persuasive power. This includes looking up the base rate, converting probabilities into frequencies and calculating costs in euros instead of merely estimating them by feel as a percentage.

The minimum procedure for this fits into four lines. The end of this module describes how it grows into a complete set of rules with an investment policy statement and a decision journal.

schritte.text: Write down exactly what triggered the impulse, for example a price alert, a headline, a conversation or the colour in the portfolio. This happens before the justification takes shape.
Note the date and time; the waiting period ends 24 hours later. Until then there is no order and no look at the portfolio.
Put a figure in euros on tax, spread and re-entry. Add a question that leaves the purchase price aside: “Would I buy this position again today at this price?”
If the decision still stands once the waiting period has ended, it is carried out and filed with the date. If it falls away, that is also a result and evidence for next time.

bloecke.md:
## Tax consequences of a sale

System 1 regularly fails at the counter-calculation because it cannot do arithmetic. In Germany, a sale is not a neutral event for tax purposes. It immediately triggers tax on the entire accumulated gain.

An equity ETF is worth €20,000, of which €8,000 is paper gain. The saver's allowance (Sparer-Pauschbetrag) of €1,000 under Section 20(9) EStG (Income Tax Act) has not yet been used.

- After the partial exemption (Teilfreistellung) of 30% for equity funds under Section 20(1) InvStG (Investment Tax Act), €5,600 is taxable.
- After deducting the saver's allowance, €4,600 remains.
- The flat-rate withholding tax (Abgeltungsteuer) of 25% (Section 32d(1) EStG) comes to €1,150, plus 5.5% solidarity surcharge, that is €63.25.
- The tax totals €1,213.25, or around €1,288 with 9% church tax.

After the sale, €18,786.75 remains instead of €20,000. Selling and buying back only pays off if the price falls by at least 6.1%. This does not save the tax, because the sale brings it forward. After the buyback, the buyback price counts as the new purchase price, which is higher than the old one. On the next sale, therefore, only the gain above this price is taxed.

bloecke.titel: Portfolio value when holding and when selling and buying back (illustrative calculation, euros)
bloecke.unter: Position of €20,000 with a paper gain of €8,000. After a sale, €18,786.75 remains after tax, regardless of how the market develops afterwards. Selling and buying back only pays off if the fall is greater than 6.1%.

bloecke.md: System 1 regularly gets two further rules wrong. For partial sales, the FIFO principle of Section 20(4) EStG applies. Under it, the units bought first are deemed to have been sold first, which, where prices have risen over the years, usually means those with the highest paper gain, and not the ones you sold in your head. In addition, under Section 20(6) EStG, losses from selling individual shares can only be offset against gains from share sales, not against interest, dividends or fund gains. An investor who sells in the heat of the moment to “at least save tax” may create a loss that lies unused in the loss pot for years.

The distinction is a teaching model and does not describe the anatomy of the brain. Part of the literature on which *Thinking, Fast and Slow* builds has not held up in the replication crisis. Kahneman himself publicly admitted to having placed too much trust in the priming chapter, because the underlying studies had samples that were too small. The Dunning-Kruger effect, the endowment effect and ego depletion are also now regarded as wholly or partly called into question.

The findings mentioned here that rest on large samples and field replications remain robust, namely framing, anchors, the neglect of base rates, loss aversion and defaults. Behavioural finance is a science whose results are checked and corrected. The direction of the findings is right, but individual effect sizes are smaller than in popular accounts.

The stock exchange is an environment with late feedback overlaid by chance. It is precisely there that System 1 is at its fastest and least reliable, yet it feels most competent. What helps are precautions fixed in advance, namely a waiting period, putting things in writing and doing the calculation.

mitnehmen: System 1 always answers, and immediately, while System 2 usually just justifies after the event what has long since been decided.
Reliable intuition requires a regular environment and quick, unambiguous feedback, and the stock exchange lacks both.
Difficult questions are replaced unnoticed by easy ones, for example “How likely?” by “How easy to imagine?”
Knowing about cognitive biases barely changes your own behaviour; what works instead are delay, putting things in writing and defaults such as the savings plan.
In Germany, a sale on impulse immediately costs tax: around €1,213 on a paper gain of €8,000 in an equity fund.

begriffe.text: The fast, automatic and effortless mode of thinking. It works associatively, is always active and supplies an answer immediately, even to questions it cannot actually answer.
The slow, rule-based and effortful mode of thinking. It calculates, compares and checks, but is only switched on when some occasion forces it to be.
The unnoticed swap of a difficult question for an easy one, for example of “How likely is a crash?” for “How easily does a crash come to mind?”
The urge to do something under uncertainty instead of waiting. It is most expensive when doing nothing would be the best option.
The bias of recognising cognitive biases in others while overlooking them in yourself. It makes mere knowledge of biases largely ineffective.
